# Incident Report: Koi Stealer Infection — 2024-09-04

## Victim Host

| Field | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **172.17.0.99** | Consistent source IP across all C2/beacon traffic |
| MAC address | **18:3d:a2:b6:8d:c4** | ARP (`arp.src.proto_ipv4==172.17.0.99`), DHCP request, and `eth.src` on all frames from this IP all agree |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-RNVO9AT** | DHCP `dhcp.option.hostname`, NBNS registration (`DESKTOP-RNVO9AT<00>`/`<20>`), and DNS self-registration queries (`DESKTOP-RNVO9AT.bepositive.com`) |
| Logged-in Windows user | **afletcher** | Kerberos `CNameString` in AS-REQ/TGS-REQ traffic from 172.17.0.99 to the domain controller |
| AD domain / DC | `bepositive.com`, DC hostname `WIN-CTL9XBQ9Y19` (172.17.0.17) | LDAP/Kerberos SRV lookups, NBNS |

## Malware Family

**Koi Stealer** (Win32/Koi Stealer). Attribution is **signature-confirmed**: Suricata/ET rule `ETPRO TROJAN Win32/Koi Stealer CnC Checkin (POST) M2` fired 48 times directly on the `POST /foots.php` traffic from 172.17.0.99 to 79.124.78.197 (corroborated by `ET INFO GENERIC SUSPICIOUS POST to Dotted Quad with Fake Browser 1`, 50 hits, same flow).

Independently verified in the raw packets: the beacon body format follows the pattern `<code>|<bot-GUID>|<random-token>|<base64/binary-blob>`, e.g.

```
101|30168213-3be0-a751-81a0-cf3b228c8654|5LHtVruc|f3f3oMg2lz4XGyHy0LidzFiNvSftke//k+COyrO9aBI=
```

The bot GUID `30168213-3be0-a751-81a0-cf3b228c8654` is consistent across the entire beacon session on this host. Requests use a static Internet Explorer 7 spoofed User-Agent (`Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 7.0; Windows NT 10.0; ...)`) on a modern OS, and the destination is a bare IP address rather than a resolved domain — both classic C2 tells.

**Likely delivery vector:** at 21:35:04 UTC+4, ~3 seconds before the first C2 beacon, the host opened a 719 KB TLS 1.3 session (SNI `www.bellantonicioccolato.it`, IP 46.254.34.201:443) that ran for ~102 seconds. Its size and timing strongly suggest this is the payload drop, but the session is TLS-encrypted and no DNS query for that domain appears in the capture (resolution occurred outside the capture window), so I cannot extract a file name or hash from it — flagged as **behavioral evidence only**, not confirmed.

Note on the earlier `GPL NETBIOS SMB` / `GPL RPC kerberos principal name overflow` alerts (17:33-17:34 UTC) against the domain controller 172.17.0.17: these are consistent with routine SMBv1/NTLMSSP/Kerberos domain traffic (all `ET POLICY Reserved Internal IP Traffic` scored) and show no corresponding malicious payload in the packets. Treated as benign/false-positive noise, not part of the intrusion.

## Indicators of Compromise
